positioning_document.title: Write a self-contained, evidence-backed positioning document
positioning_document.prompt:
Write the five Positioning Document fields for [product] on [client board]: Positioning Statement, ICP Positioning, Category Positioning, Competitive Positioning and Value Positioning. Internally read the selected ICP, category, competitive position, problems, values and product architecture. Confirm the active product and preserve selections. Use XYZ wherever the subject company needs to be named; keep the product name separate. Do not rename the client or replace competitors' identities in underlying data.

Write a concise, self-contained final narrative. No canvas references, internal IDs, source links, citations, reviewer names, review counts, sample-size discussion or research-process commentary in the output. Evidence remains internal and provides direction; do not impose a fixed review-count threshold in this document-writing task or automatically commission more research. Future research can expand independently.

Positioning Statement: who XYZ serves, the category of solution and the specific problem/mechanism/benefit.
ICP Positioning: describe the target department's people, processes, technology, inputs and buying situation.
Category Positioning: sell why this category of solution is the right fit for this ICP. Explain what competitors in the category have in common: typical product architecture, technology components and operating processes, and why these address the ICP's needs better than the relevant alternatives. Discuss shared patterns, not a vendor list or a maturity ranking. Do not imply every vendor has identical capabilities or invent a shared implementation stack.
Competitive Positioning: explain XYZ's particular approach within that category and the mechanism behind its proposed advantage; do not confuse category benefits with unique differentiation.
Value Positioning: link each problem to what XYZ does, the customer benefit, monetary mechanism and strategic benefit. Distinguish basics from remaining gaps.

Keep claims logical: problem → specific capability → how it works → benefit, using internal proof to determine what can be asserted. Do not invent shipped functionality, technologies, customer results, superiority or numbers. A proposed architecture is not proof of delivery. Where necessary use one short qualification for proposed capabilities, rather than repeating disclaimers or proof checklists throughout the document. Do not add fresh research or unrelated detail unless needed to resolve a material gap.

Update only the active product's document and editable prompt. Preserve internal evidence, source metadata, other tabs and products. Guard against concurrent edits and verify the saved result.

positioning_canvas.title: Research and fill the Positioning Canvas
positioning_canvas.prompt:
Fill the requested sections of the Positioning Canvas for [product] on [client board] in [market]. Confirm the active product, read its Product Architecture and current selections, and preserve unrelated work and other products. If ICP/category are unselected, map the options first and leave selection to the user.

ICP: map the relevant department from primitive to mature operating models. People = roles/counts; Process = how work is done; Technology = existing tools; Input = workload/population served. For payroll, People means HR/payroll staff and Input means employee headcount. Staffing ranges are illustrative. Treat the four columns as independent lists: add any number of rows, leave unused cells blank, never pad/repeat content to fill a row, and state a shared headcount once.

Categories: map the solution families serving these ICPs, including primitive substitutes. Explain overlaps rather than imposing fixed headcount boundaries. Distinguish software from outsourced services. Competitive positioning: research current peers in the selected category and give each a concise architecture description. Group architectures into evolution patterns on the relevant axis; vendors can span patterns. End with our proposed position, but verify our actual capabilities before claiming superiority or uniqueness.

Problems and evidence come BEFORE values. Research actual customer accounts in review sites, forums/Reddit, interviews or accessible video transcripts, not training-data guesses, AI review summaries or vendor marketing presented as customer evidence. Require at least FIVE distinct reviewer/organisation accounts supporting each retained problem. Deduplicate the same person, reposts and syndicated reviews; five URLs repeating one account count once. Prefer selected-ICP/market matches and multiple platforms/vendors. Record a direct link (review author/date locator if no permalink), a short paraphrase, date, ICP fit, incentive/affiliation if known, and whether the issue was resolved. Do not infer prevalence from five accounts or claim different reviewers necessarily represent different organisations.

Separate BASELINE problems the category already addresses from REMAINING GAPS. For basics, use five customer accounts describing the prior burden or the benefit of an existing solution; label these solved/table-stakes needs, not current dissatisfaction or unique differentiation. For gaps, require five accounts of the actual remaining difficulty. Merge, narrow, add or remove problems based on evidence; retain weak leads separately as unvalidated, never fabricate evidence to hit five. Do not claim every product solves a basic equally well.

For each retained problem create one linked value row: functional = what we do; benefit = what the customer gets; monetary = the economic mechanism, not invented savings; strategic = downstream business impact. Label proposed capabilities and inferred benefits; distinguish parity from differentiation. Preserve selections unless asked to change them and do not modify Keywords or other sections without instruction. Save evidence and values to the active product, verify at least five distinct accounts per problem and one-to-one value links, and warn about stale open-board saves before external updates.

product_architecture.title: Build a product architecture
product_architecture.prompt:
Build the Product Architecture for [product] on [client board], using [product URL] and [target market, if known]. Read the existing architecture first and preserve existing work unless replacement is requested.

Research official product pages and documentation for this product and comparable software. Consolidate the relevant capabilities into a proposed software-module architecture. Distinguish native capabilities, external integrations and optional extensions; do not imply the product already supports every researched feature.

Create one adjustable row per workflow; the workflow itself is the process. Use only Technology and People nodes, with short, specific names. Show people only where someone supplies input, reviews or approves. Put input data and output names on connectors, not separate data or process nodes.

Arrange each workflow left to right. When one input feeds parallel technologies, stack those technologies vertically and group them under a common name. Connect their results to a shared destination or separate destinations as appropriate. Keep real dependencies in sequence, and connect related workflows. Leave enough space for readable nodes and connector labels.

Save to the Strategy Product Architecture workflow editor using product_architecture_set, not the older generic canvas. Attach a concise feature/source map to Grounded Evidences, distinguish researched facts from proposed design, and verify the saved nodes, groups and labelled connections.
